source_refs.note: Types of immunity (PDF 175-176); Figure 21.10 is replaced by the original diagram.

blocks.text: Non-specific defence (the first and second lines) is present at birth, so it is called inborn or innate immunity. Specific defence is acquired during growth and is called acquired immunity. Acquired immunity is of two types.

items: Active immunity: the body itself makes antibodies against the antigens of microbes.
Passive immunity: the person is given antibodies to combat particular microbes; passive immunity is short-lived.

blocks.text: Active immunity may be natural or artificial. In natural active immunity the body makes antibodies naturally when exposed to antigens; it is the most effective form of immunity. Artificial active immunity is gained by giving weakened antigens (vaccination), which stimulate the body to make antibodies against the real antigens.

blocks.alt: A tree. Immunity splits into inborn (innate) immunity, non-specific and present at birth, and acquired immunity, specific and developed during growth. Acquired immunity splits into active (the body makes its own antibodies) and passive (antibodies are given, short-lived). Active immunity splits into natural (after meeting the antigens) and artificial (vaccination).
blocks.caption: Types of immunity (original diagram after Figure 21.10).
blocks.long_description: Non-specific defence, the first and second lines, is present at birth and is called inborn or innate immunity; the specific defence is acquired during growth and is called acquired immunity. In active acquired immunity the body makes its own antibodies against antigens; in passive immunity a person is given antibodies against particular microbes, and the protection is short-lived. Active immunity is natural when the body makes antibodies after meeting the antigens, the most effective form, or artificial when weakened antigens are given by vaccination.
